title: A 2,200-Year-Old Celtic Coin Hoard Emerges in Hungary
summary:
Archaeologists in Hungary have discovered a stash of more than 200 Celtic silver coins that are over 2,000 years old. It is one of the largest hoards found there in decades. The coins were unearthed during excavations ahead of construction for an electrical substation in western Hungary between 2023 and 2025, according to a translated statement from the power company E.ON.

The hoard dates to sometime between the late second century B.C. and the early first century B.C. It weighs roughly 4.4 pounds, and as raw silver alone it is worth more than $2,000 in today's market. Its rarity and historical value make it effectively priceless, the statement said.

Archaeologists first found a few coins, then searched the area with metal detectors, which led them to the hoard. The treasure had been packed inside a small ceramic vessel and sat about 16 inches below ground. Eszter Kreiter, an archaeologist at Hungary's National Archaeological Institute, called it a rarity in Europe, adding that the last similar find in Hungary was made in the late 1960s.

The silver coins are modeled on Greek tetradrachms, a very early type of large silver coin introduced in the late sixth century B.C. These copies are a type known as 'Velem,' named after Velem-Szent Vid, a fortified Celtic hilltop settlement about 10 miles to the west. Each coin shows a stylized head, probably the Greek god Apollo, on one side, and a helmeted rider and horse on the other.

The site holds evidence of more than 7,000 years of occupation, including a nearly 7,000-year-old polished stone chisel and a glass bead with a peacock's eye pattern that seems to have been part of jewelry from the sixth or seventh century B.C. A Roman-era villa was later built at the same site without disturbing the buried silver. The artifacts will become part of a museum exhibition.
why_it_matters: Buried treasure like this hoard is a direct link to people who lived more than 2,000 years ago, and studying it helps historians understand how the Celts lived, traded, and made things — knowledge that would otherwise be lost.

background_read: Archaeologists are scientists who dig up and study objects left behind by people who lived long ago, to learn how they lived.
The Celts were peoples who lived across much of Europe in ancient times, and they made their own coins by copying Greek designs, including the large silver tetradrachm.
People sometimes buried valuable things for safekeeping and never came back for them, so a buried hoard can survive underground for thousands of years until builders or archaeologists find it.
This site in western Hungary holds evidence of more than 7,000 years of people living there, and the coins were found during digs ahead of construction for an electrical substation.
